video_title: Short-Term AI Fear, Long-Term Compute Scarcity
gist: Jordi Visser argues the current AI drawdown is a liquidity-digestion event caused by a wave of capital raises (Google $80B, SpaceX $116B unlock, Chinese AI issuance) colliding with thin summer volume, not a break in the AI thesis — with 86% of S&P companies beating earnings, margins at all-time highs, and Google's cloud backlog exploding from $106B to $514B in one year. He frames the durable trade as model abundance plus permanent compute scarcity: cheaper open models like Kimi K3 expand the total market rather than destroy frontier labs, orchestration/routing wins, and physical infrastructure can never scale at software speed. He also pushes his 'QE for the mind' thesis that low-margin, labor-heavy S&P companies are the underpriced AI winners, dismisses the oil-driven CPI scare, and flags Dogecoin's record 67 days below its 20-day moving average as evidence retail is still absent.

insights.claim: The Russell 2000 (IWM) has posted four consecutive weeks with sub-1% absolute moves while small caps outperform the broader market, which Jordi Visser reads as a symptom of earnings strength and breadth broadening rather than a defensive rotation.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Compressed small-cap volatility alongside relative outperformance is an unusual combination — it argues against positioning for an imminent risk-off break and favors adding breadth exposure over index hedges.
insights.quote: IWM, the fourth week in a row with a sub 1% absolute return move. So it's been down four weeks in a row, less than 1% each move. You don't see that kind of movement anywhere.

insights.claim: After a V-shaped momentum washout of the magnitude just seen in tech momentum, Jordi Visser assigns very little chance of a straight-line recovery and expects the entire second half of the year to be spent chopping, with beat-and-raise names like Intel and Micron bottoming first while non-qualifiers lag.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Implies a stock-picking, dispersion-friendly regime through year-end rather than a beta chase — favors buying quality beats into weakness and avoiding index-level directional bets.
insights.quote: After you have a massive move of this size with the V. The way I've shown it, I find very little chance that we go straight back up.

insights.claim: Market breadth reached its highest level since July 10 with roughly 30% of names still below their 20-day moving average, and Jordi Visser treats a head-and-shoulders neckline break that then turns back up — which has now occurred — as one of the most powerful bullish signals inside a structural bull market.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete confirmation trigger to watch: a further rise in the percentage of names above the 20-day next week would mark the first technical all-clear for re-risking.
insights.quote: some of the most powerful signals come from breaking the neckline and then turning back up. Now we've done that so far.

themes.theme: Earnings Beat Rate and All-Time-High Margins

insights.claim: With almost a third of S&P 500 companies reported, 86% have beaten estimates versus 3% in line and 11% missing — an 8:1 beat-to-miss ratio against one-year, five-year and ten-year beat averages of 80%, 78% and 76%.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: An above-trend beat rate this deep into reporting undercuts the recession narrative and argues the drawdown is positioning/liquidity driven, not fundamentals driven.
insights.quote: we're on an 8:1 ratio of beats to misses

insights.claim: S&P 500 net profit margins are running near 14.4% excluding a one-off Google item and are still rising, while GDP-derived corporate profit margins sit at all-time highs — and because margins and profits historically roll over well before recessions begin (as they did ahead of the dot-com bust), Jordi Visser argues a bearish bet today is a low-probability trade.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Gives a falsifiable leading indicator to monitor: turn bearish only when profit margins and absolute profits start declining, not when spreads or oil wobble.
insights.quote: If you're going to get bearish on this, you're taking a low probability bet. Is it possible? Yes. Is it probable? No.

insights.claim: Three-month estimate revisions have been the dominant equity factor since roughly 2010 and typically deteriorate before stocks fall, and they currently show no weakness — forward quarterly EPS has been revised up to about 305.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Offers a single monitorable factor for timing a genuine regime shift; investors should watch three-month revisions roll over before cutting AI/equity exposure.
insights.quote: estimate revisions have been the dominant factor to follow. And right now they're just saying that stock market's fine.

insights.claim: China has unleashed broad state support to halt its tech selloff — state-owned funds bought nearly 9 billion shares, five state-backed insurers pledged to keep boosting equity holdings, and listing standards are being loosened so new companies enter indices faster — because with home prices falling every month, equities are the only asset class left to deliver the stability the state needs.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Creates an implicit state put under Chinese tech equities, meaning China-linked AI drawdowns are likely to be bought — relevant for anyone sizing China AI exposure or shorting Chinese tech.
insights.quote: China unleashes broad state support to halt the tech selloff

insights.claim: DeepSeek closed a funding round of over $7 billion in June in which the Chinese state-backed entity was the only outside party granted voting rights, which Jordi Visser cites as proof that China's AI effort cannot be analyzed as a private-sector phenomenon separate from the state — and notes DeepSeek's founder's hedge fund slumped 16% in the selloff.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: If Beijing is the marginal capital provider to China's flagship AI lab, US-China AI competition is a state-vs-capital-markets contest — meaning Chinese labs are far less sensitive to funding-market stress than US private labs.
insights.quote: China's statebacked nor basically the government is the only outside party given voting rights. This is why you can't separate the race.

insights.claim: The simultaneous wave of AI capital raises — Google's $80 billion, SpaceX's $116 billion unlock, Moonshot seeking a $50 billion pre-IPO valuation, DeepSeek's fresh raise, plus pending OpenAI and Anthropic needs — is soaking up market liquidity during the lowest-volume period of the year, which Jordi Visser identifies as the mechanical cause of the drawdown rather than any deterioration in AI fundamentals.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Frames the selloff as a supply-of-paper problem with a natural expiry once issuance is digested — argues for accumulating on weakness rather than de-risking, and for watching the issuance calendar as the timing signal.
insights.quote: It should not be surprising to anyone that the market's having trouble as all of this liquidity is being soaked up by issuance.

insights.claim: Google's cloud backlog grew from $106 billion to $514 billion in a single year — up another $50 billion in the quarter — with management expecting to recognize just over half, roughly $260 billion, in the next twelve months, alongside 82% cloud revenue growth, 24% aggregate revenue growth, 17% search growth and 13% YouTube ads growth.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: If roughly $260 billion of contracted revenue converts against ~$200 billion of planned capex, the bear case built on a single quarter's free cash flow print is looking at the wrong side of the ledger.
insights.quote: To go from 106 billion to 514 in one year is unprecedented.

insights.claim: Google's first negative free cash flow quarter came from $39 billion of operating cash flow against $45 billion of capex, which Jordi Visser argues is a deliberate choice rather than distress — and he flags that the headline EPS was inflated by roughly $99 billion of gains on equity stakes, with operational EPS closer to 2.85 and slightly below consensus.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: The genuinely soft datapoint is the operational EPS miss, not the viral negative FCF headline — investors reacting to the wrong number are creating the entry point.
insights.quote: they're not trying to manage towards nearterm positive free cash flow

insights.claim: Jordi Visser rebuts Bob Elliott's bear case — that Google generated only $30 billion of excess cloud earnings since Q1 2024 against $140 billion of capex — by arguing that capex is an investment whose output is the backlog, so an apples-to-apples comparison must include backlog growth, with returns materializing over a five-to-seven-year depreciation window if conversion rates hold.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A reusable lens for every hyperscaler print: judge AI capex against contracted backlog growth over the depreciation window, not against trailing cash earnings, or you will systematically underprice exponential curves.
insights.quote: investors often lag exponential curves and sustained execution removes doubt

insights.claim: Jordi Visser puts roughly 70-75% odds that Google's capex program proves value-accretive over a three-to-five-year horizon, with the residual 25-30% risk resting on three specific things: chip obsolescence if useful lives are four rather than six-plus years, roughly $1 trillion of off-balance-sheet commitments across the hyperscalers, and backlog concentration if the $514 billion is mainly OpenAI and Anthropic.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Gives an explicit probability frame and three monitorable kill-switches — the trade thesis breaks on contracted demand stalling or an OpenAI funding failure, not on any single FCF print.
insights.quote: The verdict flips not on any single FCF print but on whether contracted demand continues.

insights.claim: Synthesizing three separate podcast conversations into one context window, Jordi Visser extracts a converging consensus: models are commoditizing toward similar capabilities at collapsing prices, compute stays scarce, enterprise adoption shifts from token maxing to token efficiency, and routing/orchestration to the best model is the structural winner — meaning cheaper models expand the total market rather than destroy frontier labs.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Argues against shorting frontier labs on open-source price competition and toward owning the orchestration/routing layer and the compute underneath it.
insights.quote: don't sit there and say cheaper models are going to destroy anthropic. That's not the case. It's going to expand the total market.

insights.claim: Jordi Visser is explicitly not a bear on Anthropic but believes its growth rate will never reach the levels being discussed just a month ago, and treats the emergence of claims that 'Anthropic is done' as a sentiment signal that increases his interest in buying.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Separates a valid deceleration call from an invalid terminal-decline call — useful for pricing AI-adjacent private marks and for fading capitulation headlines.
insights.quote: I am not a bear on anthropic but I do believe their growth rate will never get to the levels that people had talked about just a month ago

insights.claim: Kimi K3 is not a small-parameter model and requires enormous compute to run, so Jordi Visser argues cheap Chinese open models are potentially negative for OpenAI and Anthropic while being net positive for essentially every other company in the world — and Moonshot pausing Kimi subscriptions because demand exceeded capacity is direct evidence that cheaper models increase rather than reduce compute demand.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Kills the 'DeepSeek moment destroys compute demand' reflex — an open-model release that forces subscription pauses is a bullish datapoint for chips, memory and infrastructure.
insights.quote: You can't be a company and be running out of compute. Sorry, it doesn't work that way.

insights.claim: GPU availability is tightening back up toward prior extremes after a brief window of slack, and Nvidia's Vera Rubin is in full production with reported capacity of up to a thousand racks per day, which Jordi Visser translates to roughly $630 billion per quarter.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Re-tightening GPU availability during an AI sentiment trough is the cleanest tell that the demand side has not cracked; Vera Rubin ramp confirmation also refutes speculation of a production delay.
insights.quote: I've seen no proof yet that anything can keep up with the demand.

insights.claim: Compute is scarce enough that Google is renting Nvidia chips from SpaceX for roughly $920 million a month, while Meta is renting out compute it cannot yet use because it lacks a cloud business — a two-sided arbitrage Jordi Visser says makes sense for both parties given the margins involved.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A secondary compute-rental market at ~$920M/month run-rates is a hard, observable price signal of scarcity — and creates an underappreciated revenue line for compute holders without cloud businesses.
insights.quote: They're literally renting Nvidia chips from SpaceX for roughly 920 million a month.

insights.claim: Jordi Visser expects a step-up function in optical and photonics earnings that has not yet flowed through, is looking specifically for beats large enough to force significant upward revisions, keeps Marvell as his largest position, and bought another optical name, AOI, this week off a technically large correction.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Concrete positioning: the trade is upward estimate revisions in optics/photonics tied to the Vera Rubin and 800 VDC buildout, played through corrected names rather than the hyperscalers themselves.
insights.quote: It's the reason why Marll is still my biggest position. I believe we're going to see a step up function in optical and photonics.

themes.theme: QE for the Mind: Low-Margin AI Winners

insights.claim: Jordi Visser's 'QE for the mind' framework holds that AI is doing for expenses what ZIRP did for balance sheets — where companies once borrowed at 2% to buy back stock yielding 6%, a mere 5% reduction in expenses now yields roughly a 20% EPS jump, making operating leverage the new financial leverage.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Reframes the AI trade from selling picks-and-shovels to owning the expense-heavy adopters whose EPS is most convex to modest cost reduction.
insights.quote: You get far more leverage with reducing your expenses through AI and how it flows to the top to the bottom line.

insights.claim: Citing Daniel Cornum's work via Aaron Levie, Jordi Visser argues low-margin businesses may become the biggest AI winners because a cost reduction of less than 1% of revenue can lift profits by more than 25% when existing margins are thin — and a screen for S&P 500 companies fitting that frame surfaced UPS, Cisco, Jabil, Centene and Walmart.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A named, screenable long list of non-tech AI beneficiaries whose margin upside is not yet in consensus estimates — the opposite of crowded AI positioning.
insights.quote: even at a cost reduction of less than 1% of revenue, it can increase profits by more than 25% because existing margins are so thin

insights.claim: Jordi Visser argues the binding constraint on enterprise AI value capture is employee adoption, and the fix is to embed agents into workflows rather than train workers on tools — treating AI as infrastructure rather than software — which means the profit-margin benefit has not yet arrived for the majority of the world's largest-revenue companies.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: If the margin benefit is entirely ahead rather than behind, current all-time-high margins are a floor, not a peak — and the agentic adoption inflection is the catalyst to track.
insights.quote: The central takeaway is that AI should be deployed as infrastructure, not merely software.

insights.claim: Crude is back near its highs around 78 versus a 2023-2024 midpoint near 68, but one-year inflation swaps and two-year breakevens have not budged, and the first non-zero CPI print from this oil move would not arrive until mid-September — which Jordi Visser uses to argue the inflation scare is not tradable.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Positions against the reflexive oil-to-inflation-to-Fed trade; the market-based inflation expectation measures are the tell, and by mid-September oil may already be lower.
insights.quote: Smart people are not paying attention to what oil is doing and saying the inflation's going higher.

insights.claim: With forward guidance suspended, markets now price roughly a 35-36% chance of a July Fed hike and global rates are rising, but Jordi Visser argues a hike would not kill the market and that the labor market is not strong on either median wages or labor force participation — while dismissing widening hyperscaler credit spreads and Oracle's blown-out CDS on a $7 billion guarantee as trivially small relative to a market of hundreds of billions.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Argues against buying credit protection or de-risking on hyperscaler spread widening, since these are the strongest balance sheets in the world and the labor data caps the Fed's hawkish path.
insights.quote: if you're betting against bonds, because the hyperscalers bonds are widening, they are the best balance sheets in the world bar none

themes.theme: Crypto Rails and the Missing Retail Bid

insights.claim: Jordi Visser argues investors who are not studying crypto now will spend the next year playing catch-up, because the blockchain is being accepted by Japan, Korea, Russia and effectively every country while the Clarity Act advances — and he links crypto volume growth directly to agentic AI, arguing consumer agents have been slow to arrive because they require massive persistent memory of a user's entire history, and that once they exist crypto transaction volumes explode.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Positions crypto as the settlement layer for agentic commerce — a second-order AI trade where the catalyst is consumer agent memory capability, not regulatory headlines; note Clarity Act odds fell back to the 30s despite Bessent's 'one yard line' comment.
insights.quote: everyone's in a race just like in AI to see who's going to own something that is equally as important as AI, which is the global financial system

insights.claim: Bitcoin has held its gains and is stable around 64,000 with Ethereum bouncing off the lows, but Jordi Visser insists both remain in a bear market until they reclaim their 200-day moving averages — and points to Dogecoin having spent 67 days below its 20-day moving average, the longest stretch in its history, as proof that retail energy is still non-existent.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Gives two clean, checkable triggers for a crypto and broader risk-appetite regime change: BTC/ETH reclaiming the 200-day, and Dogecoin closing above its 20-day after a record 67-day absence.
insights.quote: The energy in retail is still non-existent until we start seeing Dogecoin trend positively.
